sentence: The lights are on and I can hear the vacuum cleaner, so someone ___ be at home.
explanation: Evidence-based certainty uses 'must': must be at home.

sentence: That ___ be Sarah at the door — she is in Berlin until Friday.
explanation: 'Can't' expresses logical impossibility: can't be Sarah.

sentence: Where is Anna? I am not sure — she ___ be in the library.
hint: an uncertain possibility, not really sure
explanation: 'Might' expresses a possibility the speaker is unsure about: might be.

sentence: He ___ be hungry — he has just eaten a three-course meal.
explanation: 'Can't' rules out the possibility based on evidence: can't be hungry.

sentence: You have been travelling all day, so you ___ be exhausted.
hint: an obvious conclusion from known facts
explanation: A logical conclusion from known facts uses 'must': must be exhausted.

sentence: This bill ___ be right — we only ordered two coffees.
hint: an obvious mistake, so it is impossible
explanation: 'Can't' shows the speaker believes something is not possible: can't be right.

sentence: Her car is not in the car park and her office light is off, so she ___ home.
hint: a confident conclusion about the past
explanation: A confident conclusion about the past uses 'must have' plus the participle: must have gone.

sentence: There ___ be a mistake — I ordered the vegetarian option.
explanation: 'Must' expresses the speaker's certainty about a present situation: must be.

sentence: I do not know whose coat this is — it ___ belong to one of the guests.
explanation: 'Might' hedges a guess when the speaker is not sure: might belong.

sentence: It ___ be the postman — he has already been this morning.
hint: ruled out by what already happened
explanation: Evidence that rules something out uses 'can't': can't be.

sentence: The ground is wet, so it ___ have rained overnight.
explanation: 'Must have' plus the participle draws a certain conclusion about the past: must have rained.

sentence: She ___ have received your email — her inbox was full last week.
hint: ruled out as a past possibility
explanation: 'Can't have' plus the participle rules out a past possibility: can't have received.

sentence: He ___ have missed the train — he left home two hours early.
explanation: 'Can't have' expresses near-certainty that something did not happen: can't have missed.

sentence: They left at nine and the journey only takes an hour, so they ___ have arrived by now.
hint: a certain past completion by now
explanation: 'Must have' expresses confidence about a past event: must have arrived.

sentence: I have no idea where he is — he ___ have gone to the gym, or maybe to the pool.
hint: an uncertain guess about the past
explanation: 'Might have' expresses an uncertain guess about the past: might have gone.

sentence: You ___ have seen a ghost — there is no such thing!
hint: a past claim rejected as impossible
explanation: 'Can't have' rejects a past claim as impossible: can't have seen.

sentence: The theatre was completely empty, so the performance ___ have been very popular.
explanation: 'Can't have' draws a negative conclusion from evidence: can't have been.

sentence: Judging by the empty plates, the food ___ have been delicious.
hint: a confident past conclusion from evidence
explanation: 'Must have' expresses a logical conclusion about the past: must have been.

sentence: She is not answering her phone — she ___ have gone into the meeting, I suppose.
explanation: 'Might have' expresses a tentative explanation: might have gone.

sentence: Nobody ___ have predicted that result — it shocked everyone.
hint: it was impossible at that time
explanation: 'Could have' in negatives means it was not possible: could have predicted.

sentence: You ___ wear a helmet when you ride a motorbike — it is the law.
explanation: 'Must' expresses strong obligation, often from rules or laws: must wear.

sentence: I ___ work late every Wednesday this month; it is a new company policy.
hint: obligation imposed by an external rule
explanation: 'Have to' expresses obligation imposed by external rules: have to work.

sentence: Sorry I am late — I ___ to take my car to the garage this morning.
explanation: Past obligation uses 'had to', since 'must' has no past form: had to.

sentence: Do I ___ to bring my own towel, or is one provided?
hint: a question about necessity with do
explanation: Questions about necessity use 'do ... have to': have to bring.

sentence: You ___ to apply for a visa before you travel; the airline will check it.
explanation: 'Need to' expresses necessity and, unlike 'must', takes 'to': need to apply.

sentence: There ___ be a supervisor present when students use the lab.
explanation: 'Must' states a requirement: must be.

sentence: I really ___ stop drinking so much coffee; the doctor was very clear.
explanation: 'Must' can express strong obligation the speaker feels: must stop.

sentence: We ___ to be at the airport three hours before long-haul flights.
explanation: 'Have to' shows obligation from outside the speaker: have to be.

sentence: She ___ to pass one more exam to qualify as an architect.
explanation: 'Need to' conjugates like a normal verb: she needs to pass.

sentence: If you want a refund, you ___ keep the receipt — no receipt, no refund.
hint: a necessity that applies in the future
explanation: Future necessity uses 'will have to': will have to keep.

sentence: I ___ to wear a uniform at my last job, and I hated it.
hint: an obligation imposed in the past
explanation: Past obligation is expressed with 'had to': had to wear.

sentence: Candidates ___ switch off their phones before the exam begins.
explanation: Regulations use 'must': must switch off.

sentence: You ___ bring your own laptop — we will provide everything.
hint: no obligation, so needn't not mustn't
explanation: 'Needn't' means it is not necessary; 'mustn't' would mean it is prohibited: needn't bring.

sentence: It is Saturday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early.
hint: an absence of obligation at weekends
explanation: 'Don't have to' shows there is no obligation: don't have to get up.

sentence: You ___ pay for children under six — entry is free for them.
explanation: 'Needn't' expresses absence of necessity: needn't pay.

sentence: We ___ book a table — the restaurant is never full on Mondays.
hint: the action is unnecessary, use needn't
explanation: When something is unnecessary, use 'needn't' or 'don't have to': needn't book.

sentence: You ___ worry — I have already sent the invitations.
explanation: 'Needn't' reassures someone that an action is unnecessary: needn't worry.

sentence: Students ___ to buy the textbook; copies are available in the library.
explanation: 'Don't have to' plus the infinitive expresses absence of obligation: don't have to buy.

sentence: Tomorrow is a public holiday, so we ___ answer any emails.
explanation: 'Needn't' shows the action is not necessary: needn't answer.

sentence: You ___ decide now — take your time and think it over.
explanation: 'Needn't' removes the obligation to act immediately: needn't decide.

sentence: She ___ have brought a present, but it was kind of her anyway.
explanation: 'Needn't have' plus the participle means the action happened but was unnecessary: needn't have brought.

sentence: We ___ have hurried — the concert was cancelled anyway.
hint: the rush turned out to be unnecessary
explanation: 'Needn't have hurried' means we hurried although it was unnecessary: needn't have.

sentence: You ___ smoke anywhere inside the building — it is strictly forbidden.
hint: strictly forbidden, which calls for mustn't
explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses prohibition: mustn't smoke.

sentence: Passengers ___ open the doors before the train stops completely.
hint: a safety rule that forbids something
explanation: 'Mustn't' forbids an action: mustn't open.

sentence: You ___ tell anyone about this — it is a secret.
explanation: 'Mustn't' makes it clear the action is not allowed: mustn't tell.

sentence: Library books ___ be taken out of the reading room.
hint: a passive prohibition with mustn't be
explanation: Prohibitions can be passive: mustn't be taken.

sentence: You ___ park here — the police tow cars away every morning.
explanation: 'Mustn't' expresses a rule you must not break: mustn't park.

sentence: In this lab, food and drink ___ be brought past the reception area.
explanation: Written prohibitions use 'must not': must not be brought.

sentence: You ___ touch that wire — it carries a live current!
explanation: 'Mustn't' signals something absolutely not allowed: mustn't touch.

sentence: Visitors ___ feed the animals, however much they beg.
hint: a zoo rule that forbids feeding
explanation: 'Mustn't' states a prohibition regardless of temptation: mustn't feed.

sentence: You ___ see a doctor about that cough; it has lasted three weeks.
explanation: 'Should' gives advice or a recommendation: should see.

sentence: If I were you, I ___ take the earlier train.
hint: if I were you plus would
explanation: 'If I were you' is followed by 'would': would take.

sentence: You ___ better book now — the prices rise every week.
explanation: 'Had better' gives strong advice, often with urgency: had better book.

sentence: You ___ better not be late again; the boss is getting tired of it.
explanation: The negative of 'had better' places 'not' after 'better': had better not be.

sentence: Students ___ to hand in essays by Friday at the latest.
hint: ought to takes the full infinitive
explanation: 'Ought to' takes the full infinitive, so only 'ought' fits before 'to': ought.

sentence: You really ___ to apologise before this gets worse.
explanation: 'Ought to' expresses advice similar to 'should': ought to apologise.

sentence: We ___ hurry — the doors close in five minutes.
explanation: 'Had better' expresses urgent advice: had better hurry.

sentence: You ___ take an umbrella — the forecast says heavy rain all day.
explanation: 'Should' recommends a sensible action: should take.

sentence: If you want to improve, you ___ practise a little every day.
hint: general advice about improving, use should
explanation: 'Should' is the standard verb for advice: should practise.

sentence: He ___ spend so much time on his phone; it is affecting his sleep.
explanation: 'Shouldn't' advises against an action: shouldn't spend.

sentence: You ___ to see that exhibition before it closes — it is outstanding.
hint: a strong recommendation with ought to
explanation: 'Ought to' recommends something strongly: ought to see.

sentence: ___ we take the motorway, or will the coast road be quicker?
explanation: 'Should we ...?' asks for advice or an opinion: Should.

sentence: You ___ told me — I would have kept the evening free!
explanation: 'Should have' plus the participle criticizes something that did not happen: should have told.

sentence: She ___ have lied to the police — it was a serious mistake.
explanation: 'Shouldn't have' plus the participle criticizes a past action: shouldn't have.

sentence: They ___ have checked the dates before booking — now they have lost the money.
explanation: 'Should have' expresses criticism of something not done: should have.

sentence: You ___ have worried — everything turned out fine.
hint: the worry was unnecessary in the end
explanation: 'Needn't have' means the action happened but was unnecessary: needn't have.

sentence: I ___ have said that — I apologised immediately.
explanation: 'Shouldn't have' expresses regret about a past action: shouldn't have.

sentence: He ___ have driven so fast on that icy road — he is lucky to be unhurt.
explanation: 'Shouldn't have' criticizes dangerous past behavior: shouldn't have.

sentence: We ___ have booked — the hotel had plenty of rooms left.
explanation: 'Needn't have' shows an unnecessary completed action: needn't have.

sentence: You ___ have left the door unlocked — anyone could have walked in.
explanation: 'Shouldn't have' blames someone for a past act: shouldn't have.

sentence: I ___ have known you were in hospital — nobody told me.
explanation: 'Couldn't have' means it was impossible to do: couldn't have known.

sentence: It was careless of her — she ___ have prepared more thoroughly for the interview.
explanation: 'Should have' criticizes a failure to act properly: should have prepared.

sentence: ___ I borrow your charger for a minute?
explanation: 'May' is the polite way to ask permission: May I borrow.

sentence: You ___ use my office while I am on holiday.
explanation: 'Can' grants permission: can use.

sentence: Students ___ leave the examination room without permission.
explanation: Formal rules use 'may not' (or 'must not') to deny permission: may not leave.

sentence: ___ you mind if I opened the window?
hint: a polite request with would you mind
explanation: 'Would you mind if' is followed by the past form for politeness: Would.

sentence: When I was a child, I ___ stay up late on New Year's Eve.
hint: permission that existed in the past
explanation: 'Was allowed to' expresses past permission; 'could' is also possible: was allowed to.

sentence: ___ you pass me the salt, please?
explanation: 'Could you ...?' makes a polite request: Could you pass.

sentence: I am afraid you ___ park here without a resident's permit.
hint: permission that is refused with cannot
explanation: 'Cannot' denies permission: cannot park.

sentence: As soon as I turned eighteen, I ___ get a driving licence.
explanation: For a particular permitted act, 'was allowed to' is preferred: was allowed to.

sentence: My grandmother ___ speak five languages, but she has forgotten most of them.
explanation: 'Could' expresses general past ability: could speak.

sentence: The fire spread quickly, but everyone ___ escape.
hint: one specific achievement in the past
explanation: For one specific past achievement, 'was able to' or 'managed to' is used, not 'could': was able to escape.

sentence: I ___ see the sea from my bedroom window when I was little.
explanation: Verbs of perception use 'could' for past ability: could see.

sentence: After three attempts, she ___ pass her driving test at last.
explanation: A specific past success takes 'was able to' or 'managed to': was able to pass.

sentence: ___ you swim when you were four years old?
explanation: 'Could' asks about past ability: Could you swim.

sentence: When the lift broke, I ___ walk up ten flights of stairs.
hint: necessity created by a past event
explanation: 'Had to' expresses past necessity: had to walk.

sentence: He ___ not understand the lecture at all yesterday.
hint: an inability that existed in the past
explanation: 'Could not' expresses past inability: could not understand.

sentence: Luckily I ___ find a parking space right outside the theatre.
hint: one particular success on that occasion
explanation: One particular success takes 'was able to': was able to find.

sentence: She ___ run a marathon in under three hours in her twenties.
explanation: 'Could' describes abilities during a past period: could run.

sentence: I ___ help thinking he is hiding something.
explanation: 'Can't help' plus -ing means being unable to stop a feeling: can't help thinking.

sentence: You ___ to be more careful with your passwords.
explanation: 'Ought to' behaves like 'should' and always takes 'to': ought to be.

sentence: I ___ rather stay at home tonight, if that is all right.
explanation: 'Would rather' expresses preference: would rather stay.

sentence: You ___ better take some cash — the stall does not take cards.
explanation: 'Had better' warns about a sensible action: had better take.

sentence: How ___ you speak to me like that!
hint: outrage with the phrase how dare
explanation: 'How dare you' expresses outrage at someone's behavior: dare.

sentence: You ___ have seen her face when she heard the news!
explanation: 'Should have seen' emphasizes how remarkable something was: should have.

sentence: Need we ___ the whole report, or just the summary?
hint: modal need takes the bare infinitive
explanation: When 'need' is a modal in questions and negatives, it takes the bare infinitive: read.

sentence: It is the only blue house on the street, so you ___ miss it.
explanation: 'You can't miss it' is an idiom meaning it is impossible not to find: can't.

sentence: The medicine ___ be kept out of the reach of children.
explanation: Written instructions use 'must' for essential requirements: must be kept.

sentence: ___ you like some more dessert?
hint: a polite offer with would you like
explanation: 'Would you like' makes a polite offer: Would.

sentence: ___ I get you something from the shop while I am out?
hint: making an offer with shall I
explanation: 'Shall I' offers to do something: Shall.

sentence: Employees ___ use company computers for personal downloads.
hint: a formal prohibition with may not
explanation: Formal rules use 'may not' (or 'must not') for prohibitions: may not.

sentence: You ___ as well tell him the truth — he will find out anyway.
explanation: 'Might as well' suggests doing something because there is no reason not to: might as well.

sentence: I didn't ___ to like coffee, but now I drink it every day.
hint: negative of used to, spelled use
explanation: In the negative, 'used to' becomes 'didn't use to': use.

sentence: Visitors ___ to leave the gallery by 6 p.m.
hint: have to takes the full infinitive
explanation: 'Have to' takes the full infinitive with 'to': have to leave.

sentence: You ___ not be so hard on yourself — everyone makes mistakes.
explanation: 'Should not' gives gentle advice against something: should not be.

sentence: I ___ rather not comment until the investigation is over.
hint: a polite refusal with would rather not
explanation: 'Would rather not' declines politely: would rather not.

sentence: The report ___ to be submitted by noon tomorrow.
explanation: 'Has to' expresses obligation with a third-person subject: has to be.

sentence: You ___ have rushed the final checks — now there are errors everywhere.
explanation: 'Shouldn't have' criticizes a past action with bad results: shouldn't have rushed.

sentence: ___ we need to book, or can we just turn up?
explanation: 'Need to' is a normal verb, so questions take 'do': Do we need.

sentence: He ___ not agree, but let us ask him anyway.
explanation: 'May' expresses a possibility about the future: may not agree.
